newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Portugal said blocking ASEAN-EU treaty.
newsitem.headline: Portugal said blocking ASEAN-EU treaty.

text.p: Lisbon has effectively blocked a new treaty upgrading ties between Europe and Southeast Asian nations over the problem of East Timor, foreign ministers from Indonesia and Portugal said on Thursday.
Indonesia's Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said Lisbon was holding up a new agreement between the 15-member European Union (EU) and the seven-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

"(East Timor) was one of the issues used by Portugal to prevent a new-generation agreement to be signed by the two sides and of course we deeply regret it," Alatas told reporters after the 22 foreign ministers met on Thursday.
ASEAN groups Indonesia, Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
Portuguese Foreign Minister Jaime Gama said Lisbon was not vetoing a new agreement but was insisting that political and human rights issues be included -- a stand ASEAN adamantly opposes.

"Probably all of us want to move ahead," Gama told reporters. "But we should take into account that a (new) agreement...is clearly an agreement that also involves political issues and human rights standards."
Countries that did not want to include human rights issues in the treaty "are the ones who are putting the veto" on the new agreement, he said.
The old agreement was signed in 1980, when the relationship was largely defined by aid from European nations to some of their former colonies in Asia.
A new treaty envisages dozens of new initiatives across the political, economic and cultural spectrum, according to a concept paper prepared by an Eminent Persons Group.
A senior ASEAN official said that because the new agreement had the status of a treaty it required the signature of all members.
The official said, however, many of the projects envisioned for the treaty would be included in the final declaration from this meeting.

East Timor was not on the formal agenda at the EU-ASEAN foreign ministers meeting and would not appear in the final declaration, delegates said. Indonesia had threatened to walk out of the meeting if it was.
But Gama said Portugal was satisfied that the EU President, Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, at least referred to East Timor in closed-door discussions on Thursday.
Delegates said Van Mierlo endorsed renewed U.N. efforts to find "a just, comprehensive and internationally acceptable solution" to the problem.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Wednesday appointed Pakistan's former U.N. envoy, Jamsheed Marker, as his personal representative at East Timor talks that have dragged on for almost 15 years.
The United Nations has never recognised Indonesia's 1976 annexation of East Timor, which it invaded the previous year after the departure of Portugal, the colonial power.
Talks to find an internationally acceptable solution were initiated by then-Secretary-General Javier Perez de Cuellar in 1983 and continued by his successor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
Alatas said Indonesia was happy that Annan was giving new impetus to the talks.

"We'll have to wait when we can restart the negotiations, an indication from the secretary-general when discussions can resume," he said. "We've always stated we'll cooperate with the secretary-general to find a just and comprehensive solution."
